memoryText: Do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Nehemiah 8:10 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse was spoken to a crowd in tears. They had just heard God’s law read aloud, and the weight of their failure came crashing down. The leaders did not tell them their sorrow was wrong. They told them where it should lead.

“Do not be grieved.” The command is not to deny sorrow. It is to refuse to stay in it. Grief that leaves us stuck is not the grief God wants. 2 Corinthians 7:10 says that godly grief leads to repentance, and repentance leads to life. The next step after sorrow is not more sorrow. It is joy.

“For the joy of the LORD.” Whose joy is it? It is the LORD’s joy. Not merely the joy the people have in him, though that is included. It is the joy God himself has: in his creation, in his people, in forgiving. Zephaniah 3:17 says he rejoices over us with gladness. This day was a feast day, and their Father was glad to have them home.

“Is your strength.” The word means a stronghold, a refuge. When your joy depends on circumstances, it can be taken. When it rests in God’s own delight, it holds. The people were facing opposition, poverty, and an uncertain future. They needed a strength that did not depend on any of that.

Say this verse when you feel heavy with guilt or weariness. Let it turn your face from yourself to God. He has not given up on you. He is glad to forgive, and his gladness is where you find strength.
weekInReview: This week you walked with Nehemiah from a palace in Susa to the walls of Jerusalem. You watched him pray for four months, then pray again in a breath before the king. You saw ordinary people repair the wall in front of their own houses, and you saw the enemy change tactics from ridicule to threat to flattery to fear. You saw Nehemiah rebuke the nobles for oppressing the poor and refuse to come down from his great work. The wall was finished in fifty-two days. In Psalm 147 and Psalm 148, you heard God praised as the builder of Jerusalem, healer of the brokenhearted, namer of the stars, and the one whose name every creature is called to praise. At the end of the week, the people gathered at the Water Gate, listened to the word of God for hours, wept, were told to rejoice, kept the Feast of Booths, confessed their sins, and signed a covenant.
reflectionQuestions: Nehemiah prayed for months and also sent up quick prayers in the moment. How might you practice both kinds of prayer this week?
The returned exiles wept at the law and were told to rejoice. How does the gospel of Jesus Christ turn conviction into joy?
The wall was built by many hands, each near their own house. Where is your section of the wall, and who is working beside you?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that his joy is your strength.
Thank him for a word that convicts and comforts.
